planting.note: Set container-grown plants into humus-rich, well-drained soil in spring or fall, spacing to allow for suckering spread.

directions: Plant in average to humus-rich soil with reliable moisture, siting in partial shade to filtered woodland light where afternoon sun is softened; it tolerates deeper shade than most flowering shrubs but blooms more heavily with some morning sun. This southeastern US native suckers gently to form a low colony, producing clusters of tubular pale-yellow flowers from early to late summer that age to orange-red, giving a long, two-toned bloom display. New growth cultivars selected from this species show burgundy-black or bronze foliage that colors best with a bit more light exposure. Prune old canes to the ground in late winter to renew vigor and keep the colony tidy along a shaded border or slope.

subcategory: deciduous shrub grown for winter stem color

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in spring or fall.

directions: Site in evenly moist to boggy soil in partial shade, where this cold-hardy Asian dogwood tolerates far less light than most flowering shrubs and often colors its bark most vividly with some shade protection from harsh winter sun-scald. Small, flat clusters of creamy white flowers open in late spring followed by white to pale blue berries, but the main ornamental feature is the coral-red to blackish-purple young stems that light up the winter garden once leaves drop. Many variegated cultivars are grown for shaded borders and pond edges, pairing white- or gold-edged summer foliage with dramatic bare-stem winter color. Cut one-third of the oldest stems to the ground each early spring to keep a steady supply of brightly colored young wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs into humus-rich, well-drained soil in spring, allowing room for arching, suckering growth.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, where this Chinese relative of spirea produces long, gracefully arching canes lined with toothed, birch-like leaves. In late spring and early summer, drooping racemes of small tubular pink flowers with reddish calyces dangle along the branches, drawing bees and giving a soft, cottage-garden effect beneath high canopy trees. It spreads slowly by suckers to form an informal thicket, making it useful for naturalizing along a shaded woodland edge or shrub border. Thin out a portion of the oldest canes at ground level right after flowering to maintain an open, fountain-like habit.
